title: The birth of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: One land, two peoples, a British promise impossible to keep. How **1948** sparked the Middle East's longest conflict.

hero.hook: How a letter written in 1917 sparked the Middle East's longest conflict.

blocks.text: In the late 19th century, **Palestine** was a quiet province of the **Ottoman Empire**, predominantly Arab and Muslim, with Christian minorities and a small ancient Jewish community. Nothing suggests that this territory will become the scene of one of the longest conflicts in the world. It all begins with the meeting of two national movements demanding the same land: one born in Europe among Jews wanting to escape persecution, the other among the Arabs of the region who also dream of a country of their own. Between the two, a colonial power multiplies contradictory promises.

sections.title: The awakening of nationalism in Ottoman Palestine

blocks.text: The context changes with the appearance of **[[Zionism]]** in Europe, theorized by **Theodor Herzl** during a conference in Basel in 1897, in response to the rise of anti-Semitism. For Herzl, Jews will never be safe without a state of their own.
Theodor Herzl, although the founder of political Zionism, did not speak Hebrew and even considered Argentina as a host country, before rallying around Palestine.

The break occurred during the First World War: in 1917, the British government published the **[[The Balfour Declaration (1917)]]**, which promised a “national home for the Jewish people” in Palestine, while specifying that nothing should harm the rights of the communities already present. For Arabs in the region, this promise seems like a betrayal.

After the Ottoman defeat, the League of Nations entrusted Great Britain with the **mandate of Palestine** in 1922: London must both encourage the settlement of Jews from Europe and protect the rights of the Arab population, the majority in the territory.

In the 1930s, the arrival of the Nazis in Germany caused a wave of Jewish immigration, the **Alia**: the Jewish population increased from 8% in 1918 to more than 30% before the Second World War, worrying the Arabs of Palestine, who rose up between 1936 and 1939.
Tel Aviv, founded in 1909 on sand dunes, takes its name from a novel by Herzl: “Tel” for the ancient hill, “Aviv” for spring.

The British then limited Jewish immigration, at a time when European Jews were fleeing the Holocaust, which turned the Jewish militias against the occupier. Exhausted, Great Britain ended up entrusting its mandate to the UN.

In November 1947, the UN adopted a plan to partition Palestine into two states, one Jewish and one Arab, while Jerusalem obtained special international status. The Zionist leaders accepted this plan, the Arabs rejected it: a civil war broke out almost immediately.

blocks.caption: On May 14, 1948, David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the birth of the State of Israel, a few hours before the end of the British mandate.

blocks.text: On May 14, 1948, David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the birth of the **State of Israel**. The next day, several Arab armies invaded the territory to oppose it, but the Israeli forces, better organized, repelled the offensive and extended their control to 78% of the former Mandatory Palestine.

sections.title: The Nakba and the refugee question

blocks.text: For the Israelis, this victory ensures their survival. For Palestinians, the event has a name: **Nakba**, “the catastrophe”. Between 700,000 and 750,000 Palestinian Arabs flee or are driven from their homes, often in the hope of returning after Arab victory.

These refugees settle in Gaza, the West Bank or neighboring countries. Israel refuses their return, fearing losing its Jewish majority. At the same time, around 800,000 Jews from Arab countries joined Israel, often under duress.

In 1949, the UN created the **[[UNRWA]]** agency to help Palestinian refugees. What was supposed to be provisional becomes permanent: no agreement sets definitive borders or resolves the fate of the exiles, and the absence of a Palestinian state remains at the heart of the conflict.

events.detail: Two states are proposed, the Arabs refuse it.

events.title: Independence and Nakba
events.detail: Israel is born, war breaks out, hundreds of thousands of Palestinians flee.

blocks.text: In 1947, the UN proposed dividing Palestine into two states. The Jews accept, the Arabs refuse. The war that followed the creation of Israel in 1948 ended with an Israeli victory and the exodus of more than 700,000 Palestinians: the beginning of the Nakba and a refugee crisis that was never resolved.
